rebuke

rih-BYOOK -- from Old French, literally 'to beat back': a rebuke beats back bad behavior with sharp words. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To rebuke is to scold or criticize someone sharply.

The judge paused the trial to rebuke the lawyer for interrupting the witness again.

Worked Example

When a cadet shows up late with a sloppy uniform, the drill sergeant plants himself an inch away and delivers thirty seconds of ice-cold, cutting words that leave the whole line silent.

That sharp, stern scolding is exactly what it means to rebuke someone. Unlike 'nag,' which drips criticism over time, a rebuke lands all at once, hard and direct.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

admonish: To admonish is to correct someone earnestly, with a warning attached -- firm but caring, eyes on the future. A rebuke looks backward at what was just done wrong and strikes sharply, with little softening in it.

chide: To chide is to scold mildly, often half-smiling -- over muddy boots or a lost umbrella. A rebuke sits at the other end of the same act: sharp, stern, and delivered with real weight, meant to sting.

berate: To berate is to scold angrily and at length, hammering away on and on. A rebuke lands all at once -- one hard, direct hit -- and it need not even be loud; a judge's single icy sentence can be a rebuke.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

praise: to express warm approval

commend: to praise formally

Where it sits · how official the criticism is — scold → rebuke → reprimand

scold vs. rebuke: Scold is the everyday, home-and-classroom version of a rebuke -- an annoyed parent scolds a child over chores, while a rebuke comes down more sharply and more formally, often from a judge or a commanding officer.

reprimand vs. rebuke: Reprimand is more official than rebuke: a rebuke is any sharp scolding, while a reprimand is typically formal discipline, sometimes entered into an employee's record.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back (Latin, via Old French)

root — -buke

root — -buke: to strike, beat (Old French (buchier, 'to chop, strike'))

Put it together

Put it together: Old French rebuker joined re- ('back') with buchier ('to strike, chop') -- to rebuke someone is literally to beat their behavior back with words. The striking root -buke survives only in this word, though the re- prefix also appears in rebuff, another word for pushing someone back.

Where This Word Comes From

Where This Word Comes From: The Old French root buchier ('to chop, strike') survives in English only inside rebuke itself. Picture the original image: a rebuke chops bad behavior back the way an axe chops back brushwood. The sting of that sharp verbal blow is still in the word today.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Rebuke usually takes a person as its object -- you rebuke someone for something. Some word lists tag rebuke as a noun (as in 'a sharp rebuke'), but it is taught here as the verb, 'to scold sharply.'
